name: Fruit juice cleanse

card.summary: A days-long juice-only diet sold as a reset; no published research backs the detox or skin claims.
card.note: Risks include dehydration and metabolic problems in people with diabetes.

quick.overview:
A juice cleanse means drinking only fruit and vegetable juice for a few days, usually to detox or reset. It is popular online and among celebrities.

Health bodies such as the American Cancer Society and Harvard Health state there is no scientific evidence for the claimed benefits.
quick.mechanism: Believers say it clears toxins; dietitians say the liver and kidneys already do that work. Weight lost is mostly regained afterwards according to reviews.
quick.risks: Possible dizziness, dehydration, electrolyte disturbance and metabolic crises in people with undiagnosed diabetes; long unsupervised fasts can cause deficiencies.

lead: A fruit juice cleanse, also called juice fasting or juice cleansing, is a short diet, usually one to seven days, in which a person drinks only fruit and vegetable juices and eats no solid food. [1] People use it as a reset for a leaner, brighter, less bloated look: they hope for a skin glow, a flatter stomach and a fresh start before returning to a regular diet or training plan. [1][2]

It is promoted as a way to detoxify the body and is treated as a form of detox diet. [1][2] Proponents say periodic cleanses remove unwanted chemicals, and some detox proponents cite skin elimination and changes in body odour as evidence that the diet is working. [1][2]

Health bodies describe the evidence differently from proponents. The American Cancer Society and Harvard have stated that no scientific research supports juice-only diets for health benefits, and a 2015 review of detox diets reported no compelling evidence for toxin elimination or weight management. [1][2] No trial has examined juice cleanses for appearance outcomes.

chain: Juice-only intake for a few days
Lower calorie intake and more fluid, fruit and vegetable content
Short-term weight and bloating drop; some people report a brighter-looking complexion
angle.text: People use a juice cleanse as a short reset aiming for a leaner midsection and a fresher complexion. Reviews note that weight lost through short-term calorie restriction is typically regained after normal eating resumes.

infobox: Norman W. Walker, Jay Kordich, Joe Cross [1]

paras: Appearance goals attached to juice cleanses include a quick drop on the scale, less bloating and a brighter complexion. Detox proponents describe toxins leaving through the skin, urine, faeces and breath, and sometimes treat changes in body odour as a sign of progress. [2] Skincare and juice brands publish articles on juicing for a skin glow; the one dermatologist commenting on cleanses in a Yahoo Lifestyle piece, Stephen Shumack, said no studies show that a temporary cleanse reduces cellular inflammation or gives lasting benefits. [3]
T Nation members have posted detox-day routines, including lemon water, probiotics and short exercise sessions, and have discussed fruit-and-oil cleanses. [4][5]

Norman W. Walker designed an early mechanical juicer, the NorWalk, in 1936, and his books on raw, mostly liquid diets helped shape the modern cleanse. Jay Kordich popularised juicing in the 1990s through a New York Times best-selling book and infomercials for his Juiceman juicer. Celebrities and online users have kept juice diets in circulation since. [1] Joe Cross, known for the documentary Fat, Sick and Nearly Dead, advocates juice fasting and has described it as a reboot rather than a long-term practice. [1]

Catherine Collins, a hospital dietitian, has called detox a marketing concept rather than a physiological process, and Harvard has stated that no published research supports the safety or efficacy of juice cleanses. [1] The Mayo Clinic says there is little evidence that detox diets remove toxins, since the liver and kidneys already filter most ingested toxins. [2]

A 2015 review by Klein and Kiat found no compelling evidence for detox diets in weight management or toxin elimination. A 2017 review of weight-loss techniques noted that short-term loss from strict calorie restriction is typically regained. [2] Wikipedia also states that detox diets can lead to muscle loss and unhealthy regain of fat afterwards. [1]

Reference works list possible metabolic crises in people with undiagnosed diabetes or hypoglycaemia, dizziness or fainting from falling blood pressure, diarrhoea leading to dehydration and electrolyte imbalance, and protein or calcium deficiency in long unsupervised fasts. [1] A 2018 case report linked a green-smoothie cleanse to acute oxalate nephropathy. [2] A single-day fast is described as unlikely to cause harm, while prolonged fasting can be dangerous. [2]
No studies found on juice cleanses for appearance outcomes. Related reviews cover detox diets generally. [2]

timeline.event: Norman Walker designs the NorWalk juicer. [1]
Jay Kordich popularises juicing through books and television. [1]
Joe Cross's documentary Fat, Sick and Nearly Dead brings juice fasting to a wider audience. [1]

lore.intro: Juice cleanses appear in fitness-forum threads as a short reset or detox, alongside questions about whether the idea makes sense. [4][5]

claims.claim: A juice cleanse removes toxins and gives clearer, glowing skin
claims.believers: Detox proponents say fat-stored toxins leave through the skin, urine, faeces and breath, and treat changes in body odour as evidence. [2]
claims.experts: The Mayo Clinic says there is little evidence detox diets remove toxins; Stephen Shumack, a dermatologist, said no studies show lasting benefits from a temporary cleanse. [2][3]

claims.claim: A cleanse is a quick route to a leaner midsection
claims.believers: Users run cleanses to drop weight and bloating before events or as a diet restart. [4]
claims.experts: A 2017 review noted short-term loss from calorie restriction is typically regained. [2]

claims.claim: A cleanse works as a reboot before returning to normal eating
claims.believers: Joe Cross describes his plan as a short reboot and not a long-term solution. [1]
claims.experts: Harvard states that no published research supports the safety or efficacy of juice cleanses or fasts. [1]
